title.text:
Automation 2:
an AI workflow

objects.text: What does AI add to the same workflow, and what must a person still do?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 8 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome. Two sessions ago the rules read words. Last time we set limits for agents. Today the same twelve customer messages go through an AI workflow: the AI sorts them, drafts replies, and a person approves. Nobody builds anything. The results were recorded in advance, and I will always say whose they are. First, three questions from Session 7.

The question for today is this: What does AI add to the same workflow, and what must a person still do? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text:
Your two hours: mostly demonstration,
25 minutes for your own task

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: This is a demonstration: 25 of the 120 minutes are about your own task and decision.

slides.notes: Three parts matter most. In the first twenty minutes I draw the AI workflow and show what the AI was asked. Then thirty minutes go to the demonstration: the sort and ten drafts, read against the rules. After the break, twenty-five minutes cover the approval step and the measured comparison, and the rest is your own task and a decision.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between a chat assistant and an agent?
2.  What does a boundary for an agent say?
3.  What should an assistant do with an instruction hidden inside an email or a message?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 7. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between a chat assistant and an agent? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A chat assistant answers in a window and takes no action. An agent has a goal and tools such as read, draft, send and pay, and chooses its own steps. That is why it needs permissions and limits.

Question two. What does a boundary for an agent say? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. What it may read, write, send and spend, what a person must approve, what it must never do, and the stop conditions that make it halt and tell a person. The Tool Boundary Sheet records these.

Question three. What should an assistant do with an instruction hidden inside an email or a message? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Treat it as text from outside, do not obey it, and flag it to a person.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

AI workflow. An automation where an AI step reads the message and writes a draft, and a person approves it.

Draft. A reply written by the AI that nobody has sent yet.

Approval step. The point where a person reads a draft and chooses to send, edit or reject it.

UNSURE. The answer we asked the AI to give when it cannot tell, so that a person decides.

Baseline. How the task performs today. It is the number the new way must beat.

title.text:
The AI workflow: the AI sorts and drafts,
a person approves, then it is logged

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_486b7b1c.png
objects.alt: The AI workflow: the AI sorts and drafts, a person approves, then it is logged

objects.text: The person sits between the draft and the customer. The sort and the drafts were run separately.

slides.notes:
Here is the workflow for today. A new message is the trigger, as before. An AI step sorts it into a category, or says UNSURE. A second AI step drafts a reply from the company rules. Then a person reads the draft and sends it, edits it or rejects it.

Only then is the result logged and the reply goes out. Notice where the person sits. The AI never talks to the customer directly. The gold box is the step that makes this safe enough to use. One honest note: the sort and the drafts were separate runs, so this is the shape of a workflow and not one chained run.

runs.text: The AI reads the meaning of the text
The AI drafts a reply from your rules

objects.text: The new parts add value, and they add the need for a checker.

slides.notes:
Compare this with Session 6. On the left, three parts stay the same: the trigger, the route to a queue and the log. On the right, three are new. The AI reads the meaning of the text, which the word rules could not. The AI drafts a reply from your rules, which a rule workflow cannot do at all.

And a person approves before anything is sent. Every new capability also brings a new need for a checker, because an AI can be wrong in ways that read very well.

title.text:
The AI was given a short instruction,
five rules and five messages

objects.text: Shortened from the prompt. Claude, two fresh sessions given only the prompt, 4 November 2026, answer key hidden. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.
The rules

1 Photo before a replacement or credit.
2 Credit above UGX 100,000: Manager approves.
3 Finance confirms a payment in one working day.
4 No delivery time without Dispatch.
5 Polite and brief; say what happens next.
The messages
M03, M10, M14, M26 and M32, with the same text you saw in Session 1.

slides.notes:
This is what the AI was asked. I gave it five company rules and five of our twelve messages, the ones that need a reply from Customer Service. Rule one, a photo before a replacement or credit. Rule two, a credit above one hundred thousand shillings needs the Customer Service Manager.

Rule three, Finance confirms a payment within one working day. Rule four, no delivery time without Dispatch. Rule five, be polite and brief. I also told it to write in the name of Customer Service and called the rules fictional. I ran it twice, in two fresh sessions of Claude on the fourth of November 2026, each given only the prompt, with the answer key hidden.

slides.notes:
Before the results, here is my checklist, so you can see how I counted. A draft needs an edit if it fails any one of five tests. One, the photo is asked for before any replacement or credit. Two, no delivery time, date or the word today that Dispatch has not given.

Three, a payment says that Finance confirms within one working day. Four, no step is claimed as done that nobody did, such as we have passed it to Dispatch. We will ask is allowed. We have asked is not. Five, no action is promised that no rule gives, such as a report to the driver.

I applied the same five tests to every one of the ten drafts. Rule five from the prompt, polite and brief, is a matter of judgement, so I read it separately. This is one reader, and you may count differently.

Run 1: four of the five drafts need
an edit, and none broke a rule

objects.text: Claude, a fresh session given only the prompt, 4 November 2026, answer key hidden. My reading.

slides.notes:
Here is run one, draft by draft. For each I show what it promised, what it avoided and what I would edit. The M03 draft asks for the photo first, which is right, but adds an action about the driver that no rule gives. M10 needs no edit by my checklist, although it is the closest call: we are taking this to Dispatch says what will happen, not that it has happened.

M14 correctly puts Finance first and promises no delivery time, but it says we have sent the payment to Finance, and nobody has. M26 says we have passed the request to Dispatch, which is the same fault. M32 adds a promise to report the lack of cover. Four of five need an edit. None broke a rule that a checker can test.

slides.notes:
This table checks both runs against the rules. Photo before credit: all six relevant drafts ask for the photo first. Manager approval: both runs name it in the M32 reply, and their notes to the manager list the cases that might need it. But no message gives an amount, so both runs only guessed that a credit might pass the limit.

The AI cannot apply that rule without a figure. No delivery time: all six relevant drafts say Dispatch must check first. Finance in one working day: both state it for M14. Polite and brief is a judgement: all ten were polite, and the two M14 drafts were the longest. These are my readings, from one reader.

Two runs kept the rules and
differed in the extras they added

objects.text: Run 2: 3 of 5 need an edit
Both kept the rules. Both needed a person before sending.

slides.notes:
When two runs of the same prompt differ, that is a finding. Both kept every rule. But they differed in the extras they added. Run one added an action about the driver and a report to Dispatch. Run two added the word today. Both said that the payment had already gone to Finance, and both said Dispatch had already been asked about M26, which was untrue until a person did it.

The edits vary from run to run, so a fixed checklist beats trusting any single run. That is seven of ten drafts needing an edit, by my checklist. Another reader may count differently.

The approval step: a person reads
every draft before anything is sent

objects.alt: The approval step: a person reads every draft before anything is sent

slides.notes:
Here is the approval step drawn. The AI draft goes to a person, who reads it against the rules. There are three outcomes. Approve, and the reply is sent and logged. Edit, and the person changes it first. Reject, and the person writes the reply and logs why.

Some cases skip the AI draft altogether and go straight to a person: an UNSURE sort, a credit above one hundred thousand shillings, a message with two topics, or an instruction hidden inside a message, which you met in Session 7.

title.text:
What drives the cost: upkeep, charges
per use, the checker’s time and mistakes

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_11.90x4.25_44a337a2.png
objects.alt: What drives the cost: upkeep, charges per use, the checker’s time and mistakes

objects.text: No prices here. Ask a vendor about each.

slides.notes:
Four things drive the cost of any of these workflows, and I quote no prices. First, setup and upkeep: someone keeps the word lists and the prompts current. Second, charges per use, which are what the tool and the AI provider bill for each run. Plans change, so ask for them in writing.

Third, the checker’s time, because every draft needs a reader, and that time is often the biggest cost. Fourth, the cost of the mistake that gets through to a customer. A vendor who talks only about the first two is leaving out the last two.

title.text:

slides.notes:
Here is my recommendation for Nile Valley Foods, and it is a recommendation that I did not measure. Payment words go to Finance by a rule, because the words are reliable. The AI sorts the rest, and UNSURE goes to a person. Mixed cases such as M14 and M26 stay with a person.

The AI drafts replies and a person approves each one. Credits above one hundred thousand shillings go to the Customer Service Manager. And a person sends. This rests on twelve messages for the sort and five messages, ten drafts from two runs, for the replies. M14 and M26 were drafted to test the rules, and this workflow would send them straight to a person. Test it on your own messages first.

Write the step, your choice and one reason. It becomes the first line of your policy.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. Take your own task and split it into steps. For each step, choose. Rules, if the words are fixed and a wrong answer is cheap. AI drafts and a person approves, if meaning matters and you can check every result. A person only, if money, trust or the law is at stake.

Or not yet, if you have no key to check against or no owner. Say one step and your choice aloud, with one reason, and write it down. In Session 9 this becomes the first line of your company AI use policy.
